newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. African constitution makers told to try again.
newsitem.headline: S. African constitution makers told to try again.

text.p: South Africa's most powerful court on Friday rejected parts of a constitution hammered out by the country's first all-race parliament to entrench democracy after three centuries of white domination.

Constitutional Court President Arthur Chaskalson said the 140-page constitution failed in several respects to satisfy the minimum conditions thrashed out in multi-party negotiations leading to democracy in 1994.

The conditions were entrenched in an interim constitution drafted between 1990 and 1994 by then president F.W. de Klerk's white-led National Party (NP), Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) and a host of smaller parties.

Chaskalson added, however, that "the instances of non-compliance, although singly and collectively important, should present no significant obstacle to the formulation of a text which complies fully with those requirements".

The court faulted the proposed blueprint for permanent democracy mainly on its failure to entrench agreed fundamental rights, its failure to protect the independence of watchdogs including a public protector and auditor-general, and on the reduction of provincial autonomy.

The legislative and fiscal autonomy of South Africa's nine post-apartheid provinces was the major sticking point in two years of negotiations in a Constitutional Assembly (CA) comprising all 490 members of the National Assembly and Senate.

The court's ruling on Friday amounted to a rejection of some of the complex compromises between the ANC, which argued for a concentration of power in the hands of the central government, and the NP and other federalist groups.

Roelf Meyer, secretary-general and chief negotiator of the National Party, which surrendered power in 1994 after 45 years in government, welcomed the judgment as "a vindication of our faith in the Constitutional Court".
"I think we can be quite happy with this judgment. It shows up those who thought politicians, rather than the courts, would control the writing of our new constitution," he told Reuters.
Meyer said the court had given negotiators a failing mark on the most difficult aspect of their work -- the allocation of powers to the provinces.
But he said he was confident that the CA could reassemble and complete the job before the end of the year.
"We are going to have to think things through again, specifically in the areas of provincial powers, including police powers...and fiscal powers for provincial and local authorities," he said.
The Constitutional Court must approve the document, with a Bill of Fundamental Rights, before it can become law.

"We are unable to and therefore do not certify that all of the provisions of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa 1996 comply with the constitutional principles," Chaskalson said in the ruling of the court's 11 judges.

Though the court declined to give Mandela the go-ahead to sign the constitution into law, it said the Constitutional Assembly had "drafted a constitutional text which complies with the overwhelming majority of the requirements of the constitutional principles".

Chaskalson said the constitution failed to protect the right of individual employers to engage in collective bargaining, a major sticking point in the final days of negotiations between labour, business and politicians.
Although the court was satisfied the collective powers of provinces had not been reduced, some specific powers were substantially less than provided for in the interim constitution, he said.
A row over provincial powers was the main reason cited by Zulu leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi for leading his federalist Inkatha Freedom Party out of the constitutional talks last year.
Some political analysts said Inkatha might return to the table now that provincial powers were back on the agenda, but they said this might seriously delay a final agreement.
